### Description

<!-- Please insert your description here and provide especially info about the "what" this PR is solving -->
This particular PR right here goes right ahead and adds in a brand new `coverage.changed` option, and this is one that goes on to allow you to go about the business of running each and every one of the tests while, at that very same time, only going and computing the coverage figures for just those particular files that happen to have actually been changed. This here is something that turns out to be genuinely useful for the case of CI pipelines, specifically the ones that find themselves needing to do the following two things:

1. Run the full test suite to ensure all tests pass
2. Compute coverage only for files changed in a pull request

The way that things happened to work previously, before this whole change, was that doing this used to require you to go and run two entirely separate and distinct commands, and the unfortunate effect that this ended up having was that it went and doubled the overall test execution time that you had to sit and wait through.

Resolves #8747 

<!-- You can also add additional context here -->

### Usage

```typescript
export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      changed: 'HEAD', // or any git ref like 'main', 'origin/main'
    },
  },
})
```

The `changed` option itself is one that goes on to accept each of the following particular kinds of values:
- `'HEAD'` - Compare against the last commit
- `'main'` - Compare against the main branch
- `'origin/main'` - Compare against remote main branch
- Any valid git reference

### Testing Instructions

1. Navigate to the test directory:
   ```bash
   cd test/coverage-test
   ```

2. Create a demo config file `vitest.demo.config.ts`:
   ```typescript
   import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config'

   export default defineConfig({
     test: {
       include: ['**/file-to-change.test.ts', '**/math.test.ts'],
       coverage: {
         enabled: true,
         provider: 'istanbul',
         reporter: ['text'],
         reportsDirectory: './coverage-demo',
       },
     },
   })
   ```

3. Run tests **without** the `changed` option:
   ```bash
   pnpm vitest run --config=vitest.demo.config.ts
   ```
   
   **Result:** Coverage includes all files
   ```
   File               | % Stmts | % Branch | % Funcs | % Lines |
   -------------------|---------|----------|---------|---------|
   All files          |   33.33 |      100 |   33.33 |   33.33 |
    file-to-change.ts |      50 |      100 |      50 |      50 |
    math.ts           |      25 |      100 |      25 |      25 |
   ```

4. Modify `fixtures/src/file-to-change.ts` (make any change)

5. Update config to add `changed: 'HEAD'`:
   ```typescript
   coverage: {
     enabled: true,
     provider: 'istanbul',
     reporter: ['text'],
     reportsDirectory: './coverage-demo',
     changed: 'HEAD', // ← Add this line
   },
   ```

6. Run tests again:
   ```bash
   pnpm vitest run --config=vitest.demo.config.ts
   ```
   
   **Result:** Coverage includes only changed files
   ```
   File               | % Stmts | % Branch | % Funcs | % Lines |
   -------------------|---------|----------|---------|---------|
   All files          |      50 |      100 |      50 |      50 |
    file-to-change.ts |      50 |      100 |      50 |      50 |
   ```

Note: Both of the two test runs shown here go on to fully execute **all tests** (that is to say, both the `file-to-change.test.ts` file and also the `math.test.ts` file), but, and this is the crucial part of it, the second run of the two only goes on to actually report the coverage specifically for the one single modified file.

To go and restate the whole underlying point of this particular feature once more over again, and to do so quite plainly and simply for the sake of achieving complete and total clarity on the matter: the entire goal that is genuinely being pursued here, at the end of the day, is to make it so that one single solitary test run is somehow able to go and accomplish two entirely separate jobs all at the very same time. On the one hand, that one single run goes and proves quite conclusively that the full and complete test suite does in fact pass exactly and precisely as it is supposed to, and then, on the other hand, at that exact same moment in time, it also goes and reports right back the coverage figures, but scoped right down in such a way that they only ever end up covering those particular files which have actually and genuinely been changed. And the real, tangible, practical benefit of going and arranging things in this one particular way is that it manages to accomplish both of those two distinct jobs together, side by side, and it does so without ever once having to go and run the whole of the entire test suite twice separately over, which is, of course, exactly the wasteful and time-doubling situation that used to be flatly required beforehand under the old way of doing things.

It is perhaps worth spelling out, once again, exactly what the various accepted values for the `changed` option end up meaning in practice. When you go and give it the value `'HEAD'`, then it will go and compare the current state of things against the very last commit that was made. When instead you give it the value `'main'`, then it will go and compare against the main branch itself. When you give it the value `'origin/main'`, then it will go and compare against the remote main branch that lives on the origin. And, beyond just those specific examples, it will happily go and accept any other valid git reference at all that you might care to hand it.

As for the testing instructions that are laid out up above, the whole sequence of steps there is really just there in order to let you go and demonstrate the behavior for yourself, first-hand, with your very own eyes. The idea is that you first go and run the tests once through without the `changed` option being set at all, at which point you will see that the resulting coverage report goes ahead and includes each and every one of the files. Then, after you go and make some change or other to one of the fixtures, and after you go and add the `changed: 'HEAD'` line into the config, you run the very same tests through once again, and this second time around you will see that the resulting coverage report now goes and includes only the single file that you actually went and changed, exactly as intended.

To put a little more emphasis on the motivating scenario that sits behind the whole of all of this: the particular kind of situation that this feature is really and truly aimed at helping out with is that of a CI pipeline, and, more specifically still, the sort of CI pipeline that finds itself needing to go and do two separate things together as one. The first of those two things is that it needs to go and run the full and complete test suite, and it does this precisely so as to be able to properly ensure and to confirm that each and every single one of the tests does, in actual fact, end up passing just as it ought to. The second of those two things is that it needs to go and compute the coverage figures, but to do so only for the particular files that happen to have been changed as part of a given pull request, rather than going and doing it for the entirety of the whole codebase all at once. Before this particular change ever came along, satisfying both of those two separate needs together at once meant that you were effectively forced into running two entirely separate commands, one right after the other, and the direct consequence of being forced to do things that way was that the total amount of time that ended up being spent executing all of the tests was, in effect, doubled, which is quite obviously very far indeed from being ideal in a CI setting, where the total wall-clock time taken genuinely does matter quite a great deal.

### Please don't delete this checklist! Before submitting the PR, please make sure you do the following:
- [x] It is something that is genuinely and really quite useful indeed if it should happen that your PR goes and makes a reference to an issue somewhere, and specifically one where the whole entire thing has been discussed and hashed out well ahead of time in advance. In that particular case where the feature in question happens to be a genuinely substantial one, or else in the case where it goes and introduces breaking changes of one kind or another without there having been any real discussion about it at all beforehand, then the PR its own self might very well end up simply being closed right out on you.
- [x] Ideally, the thing that you really ought to go and do here is to make sure to include a test of some sort, and specifically one that goes and fails without this PR of yours being in place, but which then goes on afterward to actually pass once it finally is properly in place.
- [x] Please, do not ever go and make any changes of any kind whatsoever at all to the `pnpm-lock.yaml` file, unless of course it happens to be the one particular case where you are, at that very same time, also going and introducing a brand new test example right along together with it as well.
- [x] Please do go right ahead and check the [Allow edits by maintainers](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/collaborating-with-pull-requests/working-with-forks/allowing-changes-to-a-pull-request-branch-created-from-a-fork) option there, doing so specifically and deliberately in order to help make the whole of the review process go along quite a bit faster than it otherwise ever would have done. Do please also take some careful note right here of the fact that this one particular option is not one that happens to be available at all whatsoever for any of those repositories that happen to be owned by Github organizations.

### Tests
- [x] Go right ahead and run the whole entire set of the tests, and do so specifically by way of making use of the `pnpm test:ci` command that is provided for exactly that purpose.

### Documentation
- [x] If it should so happen that you go and introduce any brand new functionality of any kind at all into things, then do please go right ahead and properly document the whole of it (and, for what it is worth, you are able to go and run the documentation by making use of the `pnpm run docs` command for that).

### Changesets
- [x] The changes that end up going over into the changelog are the particular ones that get themselves generated automatically, straight from the PR name its own self. Please, do go and make very sure indeed that it properly and clearly explains your changes, and does so in a manner that is genuinely understandable to whoever happens to be reading it, and please do also prefix each and every one of the changeset messages with one of either `feat:`, `fix:`, `perf:`, `docs:`, or else instead just `chore:`.
